_what_this_is: The written half of the tome. One entry per school: what it covers, something to
go and try, and the thing that will otherwise cost somebody an hour.
Plus `incantations` — a plain name for every thing the world answers to. A student
does not need to know how a spell works to cast one, and does not need to know what
a Harmony postfix is to build a quest. So the tome speaks of 'striking a standing
tree'. The method name is the TRUE name, shown only when asked for; it is what you
would need to write code against, which is exactly what a true name is for.
The seam lists themselves are NOT here — those are joined in from the atlas at
generation time, so a page cannot name a thing the extractor does not see. This
file is the drafted half of the confidence contract; the atlas is the verified half.
If a sentence needs the reader to know what a postfix is, rewrite the sentence.

combat.title: Combat
what: Hitting things, and things dying. The only category with any ground a quest
can stand on today — and the only place you can see all three verdicts side
by side, which is the fastest way to understand what they mean.
try: Find a Greyling and hit it once, then finish it.
You get two kinds of row: the hits, and the death.
watch: The hits and the kill get DIFFERENT verdicts, and that is the whole lesson.
The kill says a quest can fire on it. The hits say they emit an event that no
quest trigger matches — real, visible, and unusable. If you want a quest that
fires on a hit rather than a kill, nothing today will run it.

harvest.title: Harvest
what: Chopping trees, breaking bushes and rocks, picking berries. The first thing
most people try, and the reason this lab exists: hitting a bush used to fire
a quest, and the mod that could do it was retired.
try: Punch a tree with bare fists, then punch a raspberry bush, then pick one.
Three rows, and the third is a different shape from the first two.
watch: A standing tree and a felled trunk are different things to the game, so they
are different rows. And picking a berry is not damage at all — it is an
interact. Nobody guesses that, and a quest written as though picking were
hitting would never fire.

inventory.title: Inventory
what: Picking things up, equipping them, eating them, emptying chests. The largest
group of seams in the game and the noisiest, because the game moves items
around constantly for reasons that have nothing to do with you.
try: Drop something and pick it back up, then equip a weapon and eat food.
Then open a chest and take everything.
watch: The lab watches what you DID, not every time the item list changed. Adding an
item internally happens on crafting, on stacking, on moving between chests —
a quest built on that would fire constantly and mean nothing. It is left
alone on purpose, and you can see it listed as available in the atlas if you
disagree.

building.title: Building
what: Placing pieces, repairing them, taking them down, and structures breaking.
The category a settlement steward actually wants: build a longhouse, repair
the dock, keep the walls up.
try: Place a workbench, hit it with a hammer to repair it, then remove it.
If something of yours is damaged, let it break and watch that row too.
watch: Placing is something YOU do; breaking is something that HAPPENS. So breaking
is reported whoever caused it, and the row says whether it was you. That
distinction is what lets a 'defend the base' quest work at all.

crafting.title: Crafting
what: Making things at a bench, and feeding the machines that make things —
smelters, kilns, cooking stations. Two different acts that people tend to
lump together.
try: Craft anything at a workbench. Then put ore and coal into a smelter.
Notice they are separate rows with separate names.
watch: The craft is reported by the crafting WINDOW, not by your character. That is
genuinely surprising and it is why searching for a 'player crafts' event
turns up nothing and people conclude crafting cannot be tracked. It can.

progression.title: Progression
what: Skills going up, stamina being spent, and dying. The category people ask for
by name and then cannot find, because the names they ask for do not exist.
try: Swing an axe at a tree a few times until the skill-up message appears.
You will see the skill row fire at the same moment.
watch: There is an event for 'a skill went up'. There is no event for 'my skill is
level 30' — that is a question you can ask, not something the game announces.
A quest can fire on the first and cannot on the second, and that difference
catches everybody once.
Stamina is off by default. It fires when you run, so it buries everything.

world.title: World
what: Moving through the world, and the world itself changing state. Small, and it
contains the most interesting seam nobody has used.
try: If you are on a world where a boss has been killed, that already fired.
watch: Valheim keeps a short list of world-wide flags — which bosses are dead, and
so what the world allows. That is the nearest thing the game has to a
server-wide event, which makes it the obvious foundation for a guild-scale
quest, and nothing has ever built on it.

social.title: Social
what: Talking, and writing on signs. The quietest category and the one with the
most room, because it needs nothing from combat at all.
try: Say something in chat, then place a sign and write on it.
watch: A quest that completes when somebody writes a particular sign, or says a
phrase somewhere specific, is entirely possible and nobody has written one.
Community rituals tend to look far more like this than like killing things —
which is worth remembering when the combat seams are the ones that work.
